deep.reconstruction:
The page lists full decimal periods of fractions k/p for the primes p = 163, 173, 179, 181 and 191. It continues the previous page, which treated 193, 197, 169, 121, 211 and 223. This is working material for Gauss's table converting common fractions into decimal fractions (Disquisitiones Arithmeticae arts. 312–318; the table is printed in Werke II).

The method is the one of D.A. art. 312ff. Let e = ord_p(10) and f = (p-1)/e be the index. Then the fractions k/p with 1 <= k < p fall into f classes, one for each coset of the subgroup <10> in (Z/p)^*. Within a class the periods are cyclic shifts of one another. So it suffices to write out the period of one representative from each coset. A dot over a digit marks where the period begins; underlined digits show the period starting to repeat.

(a) p = 163. Here ord_163(10) = 81 and f = 2. Since 163 ≡ 3 (mod 8), 2 is a quadratic non-residue, so the representatives 1 and 2 cover both cosets.
- 1/163 = 0.00 6134969325153374233128834355828220858895 7055214723926380368098159509202453987730 0 | 6134..., a period of 81 digits.
- 2/163 = 0.0 1226993865030674846625766871165644171779 1411042944785276073619631901840490797546 0 | 1226..., also 81 digits.

(b) p = 173. Here ord_173(10) = 43 and f = 4. Gauss takes the representatives 1, 2, 3, 4. My check: 2 and 3 are quadratic non-residues, and 4 is a residue but not a quartic residue; the four periods are mutually non-shifted, so the cosets are distinct.
- 1/173 = 0.0057803468208092485549132947976878612716763 | 0057...
- 2/173 = 0.0115606936416184971098265895953757225433526 | 0115...
- 3/173 = 0.0173410404624277456647398843930635838150289 | 0173...
- 4/173 = 0.0231213872832369942196531791907514450867052 | 0231...
Each is written as a 40-digit line plus a short tail such as 30·057 or 26·0115, with the dot marking the period start.

(c) p = 179. Here ord_179(10) = 178, so 10 is a primitive root and f = 1. Only 1/179 is needed: a single 178-digit period, 5586592178 7709497206 ... 6424581 00, after which 558659 &c. repeats.
- The digit 3 that ends '...20111731843' was squeezed onto the end of row 2, so row 3 begins 5754189944.
- Row 4 has one 9-digit group (324022346) because its final 3 begins the next group (3687150837).
- I checked all 178 digits by long division; they are correct.

(d) p = 181. Here ord_181(10) = 180 and f = 1. The single period of 1/181 has 180 digits, 5524861878 ... 0883977900, then 55248 &c. repeats.

(e) p = 191. Here ord_191(10) = 95 and f = 2. Because 191 ≡ 7 (mod 8), 2 is a quadratic residue, and so are 3 and 5; 7 is the least non-residue. Gauss therefore takes the representatives 1 and 7.
- 1/191 = 0.00 5235602094...6282722513 08900 | 52356, a period of 95 digits.
- 7/191 = 0.0 3664921465 9685863874 3455497382 1989528795 8115183246 0732984293 1937172774 8691099476 4397905759 16230 | 366..., also 95 digits.

The choice of 7 rather than 2 for 191, and of 1–4 for 173, shows the coset/index theory being applied deliberately.
errors: No arithmetic errors found. All digit strings agree with the exact expansions of 1/163, 2/163, 1/173, 2/173, 3/173, 4/173, 1/179, 1/181, 1/191 and 7/191.

Corrections are visible in the manuscript but the final readings are correct: an overwritten digit in 14110429 (2/163); struck or overwritten digits after 2011173184 in row 2 of 179, where the carried digit 3 was moved; a deleted digit in 9888·26815 in row 5 of 179.
The grouping in row 4 of 179 is irregular (a 9-digit group 324022346), but no digit is lost.

results.what: Complete decimal periods of k/p for p = 163, 173, 179, 181, 191, with one representative numerator per coset of <10> in (Z/p)^* (1,2 for 163; 1,2,3,4 for 173; 1 for 179 and 181; 1,7 for 191).
results.modern_name: Decimal period tables / multiplicative order of 10 mod p; decomposition of residues into cosets of <10> (index theory of repeating decimals)
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss (Disquisitiones Arithmeticae 1801, arts. 312-318; table printed in Werke II); earlier decimal-period tables by J. H. Lambert, Robertson and others, later Reuschle and Burckhardt

results.what: Choice of the least quadratic non-residue (7 for 191, 2 for 163) as second representative when the index is 2.
results.modern_name: Quadratic character and the index of 10 modulo p

deep.surprise_reason: These are worksheets for Gauss's well-known, published table converting fractions to decimals. The method is the one he explains in D.A. arts. 312-318; nothing here is new.
